content:
Quick answer: You can usually keep gardening with arthritis by pacing jobs into short sessions, changing position often, and using lightweight, padded or long-handled tools, raised beds and seating. If you take methotrexate, protect your skin from the sun. Wear gloves, keep tetanus jabs up to date and follow RHS precautions when handling compost.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against NHS physical activity guidelines, NHS medicines information on methotrexate and sun sensitivity, the NHS page on tetanus, and Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) advice on minimising health risks in the garden. We do not recommend or sell any tools or brands.

Gardening can be one of the most rewarding things you do with arthritis. It gets you moving, outdoors and absorbed in something other than pain. It can also be hard on hands, knees, hips and backs if you try to do too much at once. This guide covers how to plan your garden and your gardening sessions so you can keep enjoying it, with practical ways to protect your joints and stay safe.

Why gardening can be good for you

NHS guidance says adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strengthening activities on at least 2 days. The NHS lists pushing a lawn mower as an example of moderate activity, and many gardening tasks, such as digging, carrying and raking, also use your muscles. Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis in NICE guidance, so activity you enjoy and do regularly is valuable.

Beyond the physical side, many people find gardening helps with mood, a sense of purpose and getting outside. Thrive, the gardening for health charity, uses gardening to support people living with disabilities or ill health and offers gardening guides and advice.

Before you start: warm up and plan

  • Warm up. A few minutes of gentle movement, such as marching on the spot, shoulder rolls, and opening and closing your hands, can ease stiffness before you start.
  • Choose your time of day. If you are stiffest in the morning, garden later. Avoid the hottest part of the day in summer.
  • Plan the session. Decide on one or two jobs rather than "doing the garden".
  • Gather tools first so you are not going back and forth.
  • Set a timer to remind yourself to change position or take a break, perhaps every 20 to 30 minutes.

Pacing: the key to gardening without a flare

Many people do too much on a good day and pay for it for days afterwards. Pacing means breaking jobs into smaller chunks and spreading them out:

  • Alternate heavy and light jobs, for example digging, then potting at a table, then deadheading.
  • Alternate positions, so you are not kneeling, bending or reaching for too long.
  • Spread big jobs, such as clearing a border, over several days or weeks.
  • Stop before you are sore. If a job is causing pain that lasts more than a couple of hours afterwards, do less next time.
  • Accept help for the heaviest seasonal jobs if you can.

Our guide to pacing techniques explains how to find your baseline and build up gradually.

Protecting your joints while you garden

Hands and wrists

  • Use tools with thicker, padded or angled handles, so you do not have to grip tightly. Foam tubing can be added to existing handles.
  • Ratchet secateurs and loppers can cut in stages, needing less force each time.
  • Keep your wrist straight where you can, and use your whole arm rather than twisting your wrist.
  • Wear well-fitting gloves to protect skin and give a better grip.
  • Use both hands to carry things, and spread the load.

Knees and hips

  • Use a kneeling pad, or a kneeler with handles to help you get up and down.
  • Sit on a low stool or garden seat for ground-level work instead of kneeling.
  • Work at a raised bed or potting bench to avoid bending and kneeling altogether.

Back and shoulders

  • Use long-handled tools to avoid stooping.
  • Bend your knees, not your back, when lifting, and keep loads close to your body.
  • Buy compost and soil in smaller bags, or ask for delivery close to where you need it.
  • Use a wheelbarrow, sack trolley or garden cart rather than carrying.
  • Avoid working with your arms above shoulder height for long. Use a step or long-reach tools carefully.

Our guide to joint protection explains the principles behind these tips.

Tools and equipment that can help

You do not need to replace everything. Start with the tasks you find hardest:

  • Lightweight tools, such as aluminium or plastic rather than heavy steel
  • Long-reach tools, such as grabbers, weeders and pruners on extension poles
  • Lightweight or expanding hoses, a hose reel on wheels, or watering cans with two handles that you only half fill
  • Battery-powered tools, which can be lighter than petrol and easier to start than pull-cord tools
  • A wheeled garden seat or kneeler to move along borders
  • Tool belts or aprons to keep small tools close

An occupational therapist can advise on tools and techniques if your hands are particularly affected. Ask your GP or specialist team about a referral.

Designing a lower-effort garden

Small changes to the layout can make a big difference over time:

  • Raised beds at a comfortable height for sitting or standing. Our guide to raised beds covers heights and widths.
  • Containers and pots on stands or wheeled bases, with lightweight compost.
  • Level, firm paths wide enough for a wheelbarrow or walking aid, with no trip hazards.
  • Handrails on steps and slopes.
  • Seating dotted around the garden, so you can rest wherever you are working.
  • Low-maintenance planting, such as shrubs and perennials rather than annual bedding, and mulching to reduce weeding.
  • A water butt or tap close to your beds to reduce carrying.
  • Vertical growing, such as climbing beans or wall planters, at a reachable height.

If you rent, ask your landlord before making permanent changes.

Gardening after a joint replacement

Gardening can be a goal to work towards after surgery, but give your new joint time to heal and follow your surgical team's advice. NHS recovery advice includes:

  • After a knee replacement: avoid twisting your knee, bending down and reaching up as much as possible in the early weeks, and do not kneel on your new knee until your doctor says you can.
  • After a hip replacement: in the early weeks, the NHS advises not bending your hip more than 90 degrees and not bending down to touch your feet or ankles.

Raised beds, a potting bench and long-handled tools are especially useful during recovery. Ask your physiotherapist when you can return to heavier jobs such as digging, and which positions to avoid. Our guide to preparing for joint replacement suggests getting the garden low-maintenance before your operation.

A sample 45-minute gardening session

This is just an example to adapt to your own needs and limits:

  1. 5 minutes: gentle warm-up, such as walking round the garden, shoulder rolls, and opening and closing your hands.
  2. 15 minutes: one heavier job, such as weeding a section of raised bed with a long-handled hoe.
  3. 5 minutes: sit down with a drink.
  4. 15 minutes: a lighter job at a different height, such as potting up seedlings at a bench.
  5. 5 minutes: tidy up using a cart, then a few gentle stretches for your back, hips and hands.

Notice how you feel that evening and the next day, and adjust next time. If you are fine, you can gradually add a little more.

Getting help with the garden

If the garden is becoming too much, it is not a failure to get help. Options include family or neighbours, local volunteer or befriending schemes, gardening services, or swapping jobs with a friend: you sow seeds and pot plants for them, they do your heavy digging. If you need support at home more generally, a needs assessment from your local council may help. For many people, keeping the parts of gardening they love while handing over the hardest jobs is the best of both worlds.

Staying safe in the garden

Sun and medicines

Some arthritis medicines can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. The NHS says methotrexate can cause a sunburn-like reaction, and advises staying out of bright sun, using a high factor sunscreen of SPF 30 or above, and wearing clothes that protect you from the sun. Check the leaflet for your own medicines, or ask your pharmacist.

Cuts and tetanus

The NHS says there is a risk of tetanus if soil or manure gets into a wound, such as a scratch from a thorn. The RHS advises keeping tetanus vaccinations up to date. Check with your GP surgery if you are not sure you have been fully vaccinated. Clean any cuts straight away.

Infections and immune-suppressing medicines

If you take medicines that suppress your immune system, you may be more vulnerable to infections. The RHS notes that elderly gardeners and those with a suppressed immune system are most vulnerable to Legionella bacteria, which can be found in compost and potting media. RHS precautions include:

  • wearing gloves whenever handling soil and compost
  • not opening bags of compost with your face right over the opening
  • moistening dry potting media before use
  • considering a dust mask when turning compost or handling dusty materials
  • not storing potting media in greenhouses, where it heats up
  • emptying hoses after use and not leaving full hoses in the sun
  • washing your hands after gardening, before eating or touching your face

Get any cuts or scratches that become red, hot, swollen or painful checked promptly, especially if you take immune-suppressing medicines.

Heat, cold and falls

  • Drink water regularly and take breaks in the shade in hot weather.
  • Keep warm in cold weather, as many people find cold makes stiffness worse.
  • Keep paths clear and avoid wet, slippery surfaces. Take a phone with you if you garden alone.

During a flare

You do not have to give up entirely. Try lighter jobs, such as sowing seeds at a table, deadheading from a seat, planning next season, or simply sitting in the garden. Some people keep a few pots by the back door for days when going further is too much. Rest the affected joints, and return gradually as the flare settles.

If you do not have a garden

  • Grow herbs, salad or flowers in window boxes or pots on a balcony.
  • Look for community gardens or allotment groups, which may have raised beds or accessible plots.
  • Thrive and other gardening for health organisations run programmes in some areas.
  • Indoor plants can give some of the same pleasure with very little physical effort.

Allotments

An allotment can be a lot of work. If you have one, or are on a waiting list, ask your council or allotment society whether there are smaller plots, raised beds or plots closer to the entrance and water supply. Share a plot with a friend to halve the work.

Seasonal jobs and how to make them easier

  • Spring: sow seeds in trays at a table, and plant out in small batches over several days.
  • Summer: water in the cooler parts of the day; use mulch to keep moisture in and reduce watering.
  • Autumn: rake leaves little and often; use a leaf grabber to pick them up.
  • Winter: plan next year, clean and sharpen tools sitting down, and keep active indoors.

When to get medical help

See your GP or physiotherapist if pain after gardening lasts more than a few days, or if a joint keeps swelling after activity. Get urgent advice the same day from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever, or if a cut becomes red, hot, swollen or painful, or you are unsure about your tetanus protection. Call 999 for severe bleeding, chest pain or a fall with a suspected broken bone.

Frequently asked questions

Is gardening good exercise for arthritis?

It can be. Gardening keeps you moving and builds strength. The NHS lists pushing a lawn mower as moderate activity. Pace yourself so you do not trigger a flare.

What gardening tools are best for arthritic hands?

Lightweight tools with thick, padded or angled handles, ratchet secateurs and long-reach tools. An occupational therapist can give personalised advice.

How can I garden without kneeling?

Use raised beds, containers on stands, a garden stool or long-handled tools.

Is gardening safe if I take methotrexate?

Generally, yes, with sensible precautions. The NHS says methotrexate can make skin sensitive to sunlight, so use SPF 30 or above and cover up. Wear gloves, clean cuts and wash your hands.

Do I need a tetanus jab for gardening?

Check you are fully vaccinated. The RHS advises keeping tetanus jabs up to date. If you are unsure, ask your GP surgery.

How long should I garden for?

Start with short sessions, such as 20 to 30 minutes, with breaks and changes of position. Build up gradually.
